title: Is good SEND provision just good teaching?
author: David Didau
summary: Didau tests the staffroom claim that children with special educational needs simply need good teaching, and concludes it is largely — though not entirely — right. He works through common areas of need to show the overlap: chunked and sequenced instruction suits a child with a working memory deficit and every other child too, systematic synthetic phonics is equally the best route for dyslexic and non-dyslexic readers, and the structure, predictable routines and consistent proportionate consequences that help children with attachment difficulties, autism or ADHD improve the classroom generally. His key qualification is the distinction between accommodation, which changes how a child accesses learning, and intervention, which addresses an underlying difficulty through additional teaching — both of which should act as an on-ramp to the same ambitious curriculum rather than a detour. The argument then escalates via Nuthall's claim that ability is the consequence rather than the cause of what students learn, and Engelmann's that the curriculum largely determines how smart children become: give some children a thinner curriculum and their assessed ability becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Didau's practical conclusion is that knowledge is the one major difference between children that schools actually control, so the question is how to get as much of it into every child as possible. He ends with a warning about labels lowering expectations — permanent scaffolds, replaced texts, support sliding into dependence — and a standard for judging schools by how well they serve those least able to compensate for weak teaching.
points: The overlap argument is tested case by case rather than asserted: nothing that helps a child with a specific need is shown to disadvantage the rest of the class.
Didau's accommodation-versus-intervention distinction is the useful operational line — one changes access, the other adds teaching to address a difficulty.
Nuthall's claim that ability is the consequence rather than the cause of classroom learning is the pivot on which the whole essay turns.
The warning about labels is the practical caution — scaffolds become permanent, ambitious texts get swapped for accessible ones, and access slides into dependence.
His proposed measure of a school's teaching quality: how well it works for the children least able to compensate for its weaknesses.
quotes: You sometimes hear that children with special educational needs don’t need different provision, they just need god teaching. I think there’s some truth to this.

For instance, a child with a working memory deficit is likely to benefit from having information carefully sequenced and instruction broken into manageable chunks. But all children have limited working memory capacity and so all children will benefit from having instruction chunked.

It’s essential to distinguish between accommodation, which changes how a child accesses learning, and intervention, which addresses an underlying difficulty through additional teaching. In both cases, SEND provision should, as far as possible, act as an on-ramp to the same ambitious curriculum rather than a detour into a quiet cul-de-sac.

You may need to reread that sentence for its implications to sink in. We tend to believe that differences in children’s ability cause some to learn more and others to learn less but what Nuthall suggests is that children’s academic ability is — to some extent — a product of what happens in the classroom.

If some children are given a less challenging curriculum than others we ensure they will become less capable. Our determination of their ability to access the curriculum becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Identifying a child as having a need can — often does — lower expectations. When we rationalise why children find it difficult to engage with an academic curriculum, it’s a small step to finding reasons for them not to have to struggle at all. Scaffolds become permanent, ambitious texts are replaced with more ‘accessible’ ones and support intended to provide access slides into approaches which inadvertently create dependence.

The children who are most disadvantaged, most at risk of failing, will be those that most need their teachers to be aware of effective practice. Advantaged children are more likely to thrive regardless of what their teachers do but they too will still benefit from the kinds of practice children with SEND need. The quality of teaching in a school should be judged by how well it works for those least able to compensate for its weaknesses.
